Based on the video provided and the "Archery" file from your notes, here is a breakdown of the common "high bow shoulder" issue and how to correct it.

### The Illusion of a High Bow Shoulder

In the video, Jake Kaminski explains that if you or your coach think your bow shoulder is too high, the shoulder itself might not be elevated at all [[00:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=27&utm_source=gemini)]. Instead, it's often an illusion caused by a **tilted rib cage** and poor spinal alignment [[00:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=46&utm_source=gemini)].

* When your rib cage tilts backward (away from the target), it pushes your bow shoulder up in space, making it look high [[02:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=125&utm_source=gemini)].
* No matter how hard you try to push the shoulder down, it won't move if your rib cage remains tilted [[00:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=46&utm_source=gemini)].
* This bad alignment makes getting through the clicker very difficult and inefficient [[03:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=210&utm_source=gemini)].

This directly aligns with the "Archery" file, which notes that a very common beginner mistake is leaning back. As the archer pulls the string back, they sometimes pull their body back with it.

### How to Fix It

To fix this posture issue, the video and your notes recommend a few specific techniques:

**1. The "T" Position (Straight Spine)**
Your spine should act as a straight pivot point that your body rotates around [[05:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=308&utm_source=gemini)]. You want to maintain a "letter T position," keeping your body straight up and down. Your spine is the stem of the T, and your arms form the crossbar.

**2. Reach Toward the Target**
Kaminski suggests that you shouldn't worry about forcing your shoulder down or squeezing your lats. Instead, simply **reach as far as you can toward the target** when lifting the bow [[01:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=93&utm_source=gemini)]. This naturally sets your bow shoulder in the lowest and most optimal position [[01:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=68&utm_source=gemini)]. Make sure you don't lean forward and compromise your spine when doing this [[01:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=108&utm_source=gemini)].

**3. Shift Your Weight Forward**
Bows can be heavy, and holding that weight away from your center line naturally makes your body want to compensate by leaning backward [[04:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=281&utm_source=gemini)]. To combat this, try shifting your weight slightly onto your front foot as you lift the bow [[04:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=275&utm_source=gemini)].

**4. Record Yourself**
Kaminski recommends setting up a camera directly behind you on the shooting line [[04:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=260&utm_source=gemini)]. Watching yourself shoot can reveal subtle spine and rib cage tilts that you may not feel during the shot [[06:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EEMXB1nHmTk&t=391&utm_source=gemini)]. Using a training mirror or filming yourself on a phone between ends is also highly recommended for building better habits.
</pasted_content id="b1a4">
